title: Clean Architecture
scopeHtml: Layers and the dependency rule, model types and mappers, use cases (value vs boilerplate), Google's optional domain layer, boundaries, package structure, comparisons and migration.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the dependency rule in Clean Architecture and how it shows up in an Android codebase.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates recite "presentation, domain, data" without knowing which way the arrows point or why. The rule is the whole idea.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Source-code dependencies point only inward, toward business rules. Policy (domain: entities and use cases) knows nothing about details (Android UI, Room, Retrofit). Details depend on policy, never the reverse. When the domain must call something outward, such as saving data, it declares an interface and the outer layer implements it. That is dependency inversion, and it is what lets me test and change details without touching rules.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Uncle Bob's circles, mapped to Android:

 UI (Compose, ViewModel)  ----->  Domain (entities, use cases, repo interfaces)
 Data (Room, Retrofit, repo impl) -->  Domain
 Domain  --> nothing (pure Kotlin)

Note the arrow from Data to Domain. In a naive "layered" app, data sits at the bottom and domain depends on it. In Clean, UserRepository (interface) lives in domain, UserRepositoryImpl lives in data and depends on domain. At runtime the call still flows domain to data; at compile time the arrow is inverted. Something (Hilt/Dagger, the composition root in :app) wires impl to interface.

Consequences: the domain module can be a pure Kotlin/JVM module with no android.jar, tests run in milliseconds, and swapping Room for SQLDelight edits only the data module. The rule is enforced by module boundaries or an architecture test, not by convention.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// domain
interface OrderRepository { suspend fun place(order: Order): OrderId }

class PlaceOrderUseCase(private val repo: OrderRepository) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(order: Order) = repo.place(order)
}

// data (depends on domain, never the opposite)
class OrderRepositoryImpl(private val api: OrderApi) : OrderRepository {
    override suspend fun place(order: Order) = OrderId(api.create(order.toDto()).id)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Domain importing Room annotations or retrofit2.Response: the arrow now points outward.
  • Believing "three packages" equals Clean Architecture. Without inversion it is just layering.
  • Putting the repository interface in the data module, so use cases depend on data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who wires the implementation? → The composition root (:app with Hilt/Dagger or manual DI).
  2. Can domain use coroutines/Flow? → Yes, they are language/library-level, not framework details; domain stays JVM-pure.
  3. How do you enforce it? → Gradle module dependencies (domain has no dependency on data/ui), plus Konsist/ArchUnit-style tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE names the layers. Senior explains inverted compile-time arrows, where the interface lives, and how it is enforced mechanically.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team swapped REST for GraphQL in one sprint because only the data module and mappers changed; another team found @Entity in domain classes and could not leave Room for months.

questions.promptHtml: How does Google's recommended Android architecture differ from textbook Clean Architecture, and is the domain layer mandatory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you follow official guidance critically instead of cargo-culting a blog diagram.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Google recommends at least two layers: UI and data. A domain layer is optional, added only for complex or reused business logic. Their docs also warn that "domain layer" there is not the same as in Clean Architecture. In Google's model the data layer already holds business logic via repositories, and the UI layer depends on data directly; Clean's strict inversion is not required.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the architecture guide: UI layer (UI elements plus state holders like ViewModel) and data layer (repositories and data sources) are the baseline. The domain layer sits between them and holds use cases/interactors "for complex business logic, or simple business logic reused by multiple ViewModels". The guide explicitly notes the term differs from other architectures.

Differences:

Aspect Textbook Clean Google guide
Domain mandatory core, no outward deps optional, depends on data layer
Dependency direction data depends on domain interfaces domain/UI depend on data repositories
Repository interface in domain commonly interface in data, or concrete class
Business logic entities + use cases repositories + (optional) use cases

Both agree on: separation of concerns, single source of truth, UDF, testability. The practical stance: start with UI + data; extract a use case when logic is duplicated across ViewModels or a ViewModel gets heavy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming Google "mandates" Clean Architecture.
  • Treating every repository call as needing a use case.
  • Saying the domain layer is useless: it is optional, not discouraged.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When do you add it? → Duplicated logic across ViewModels, combining multiple repositories, heavy transformation.
  2. Does Google's domain layer invert dependencies? → No, it depends on data layer classes.
  3. Why did Now in Android add one? → To move duplicated/complex ViewModel logic into named use cases (verify current repo state).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE draws the Clean diagram. Senior says what the guide says, why the term differs, and decides per codebase.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that inflated every screen with use cases hit boilerplate fatigue; teams that never extracted any had 1,500-line ViewModels.

questions.promptHtml: Why do apps end up with DTO, Entity, Domain model and UI model for the "same" thing, and when is that justified?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes whether you understand that each model has a different reason to change.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each model is owned by a different volatile thing. DTO changes when the server contract changes, Entity when the DB schema changes, domain model when business rules change, UI model when screens change. Separate classes let those changes stay local. But four classes per concept is only justified when the shapes or change rates actually diverge; otherwise merge them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reasons to change:

UserDto      <- backend JSON (nullable, snake_case, strings for dates)
UserEntity   <- Room schema (flattened, FK ids, migrations)
User         <- business meaning (non-null, Instant, value types, validated)
UserUiModel  <- display (formatted strings, colors, @Immutable for Compose)

Real divergence examples: server sends "price": "12.50" strings and nullable fields; DB stores cents as Long; domain uses Money; UI shows "Rs 12.50". Sharing one class forces @SerialName, @ColumnInfo and Compose stability concerns onto the same type.

Pragmatic collapse: for simple CRUD where DTO equals entity equals domain, one @Serializable class is fine until it hurts. Common compromise: DTO + Entity in data (mapped internally), domain model exposed, UI state built from domain directly (skip UiModel unless formatting is non-trivial). Compose adds a reason for UI models: domain classes using List or from non-Compose modules are unstable; UI models can use ImmutableList or be annotated (see the Compose stability section in A3).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Serializable data class UserDto(val id: String, @SerialName("full_name") val fullName: String?, val balance: String?)
data class User(val id: UserId, val name: String, val balance: Money)

fun UserDto.toDomain() = User(UserId(id), fullName.orEmpty(), Money.parse(balance ?: "0"))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mapping identical fields 1:1 forever with no divergence (pure tax).
  • Letting nullable DTO fields leak so domain code is full of ?:.
  • Domain model with serialization annotations.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which can you drop first? → UI model, then entity/DTO merge if the schema mirrors the API.
  2. Who owns the mappers? → The layer that knows the outer type (data owns DTO/Entity mappers; UI owns UiModel mapper).
  3. How do you avoid drift bugs? → Mapper unit tests, round-trip tests, strict nullability at the boundary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "separation of concerns". Senior frames it as change-rate isolation and says when to collapse.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A backend rename of a field broke only UserDto's mapper in one team; in another a shared annotated class made a Room migration crash the JSON parser.

questions.promptHtml: What does a use case/interactor give you, and when is it just boilerplate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most debated Clean Architecture topic. Interviewers want a reasoned position.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A use case is a single-purpose class that encapsulates one piece of application logic: combine repositories, apply rules, reuse across ViewModels. It earns its place when logic is shared, complex, or combines sources. A use case that only forwards repo.getUser() is boilerplate, and I would not write it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Value signals:

  • Logic reused by two or more ViewModels (also Services, Workers, Application).
  • Combines multiple repositories (GetLatestNewsWithAuthorsUseCase).
  • Non-trivial rules or sorting/filtering/merging worth isolated tests.
  • Needs a threading policy (Dispatchers.Default) for CPU-heavy work.

Cost signals: one file and one DI binding per call, extra indirection when navigating code, ViewModel constructors listing eight use cases, mechanical tests that only verify delegation.

Google's guide naming: present-tense verb + noun + UseCase; operator fun invoke for call syntax; no mutable data; no own lifecycle (scoped to the caller, a new instance each time is fine); must be main-safe, but check first whether blocking work belongs in the data layer if results should be cached. If Room can answer a combined query itself, a repository method is better than a use case.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class GetFeedUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val posts: PostRepository,
    private val authors: AuthorRepository,
    @DefaultDispatcher private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher,
) {
    operator fun invoke(): Flow<List<FeedItem>> =
        combine(posts.observe(), authors.observeAll()) { p, a ->
            val byId = a.associateBy { it.id }
            p.mapNotNull { post -> byId[post.authorId]?.let { FeedItem(post, it) } }
        }.flowOn(dispatcher)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One use case per repository method by policy.
  • Use case holding state (cache) so it behaves like a repository.
  • Use case taking Context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Use case returns Flow or suspend? → Match the data: stream for observed data, suspend for one-shot actions.
  2. Can use cases call use cases? → Yes, but deep chains hurt readability.
  3. How do you stop pass-through creep? → Review rule: add only when there is logic, reuse, or combination; delete ones that stay trivial.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defends or rejects use cases dogmatically. Senior gives criteria and shows the cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 60-ViewModel app had 140 use cases, 90 of them one-line delegates; deleting them cut review noise without losing any test coverage that mattered.

questions.promptHtml: How should mappers be written and what do they really cost? Extension functions, mapper classes, or a library?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks pragmatism: mappers are the visible tax of layered models.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use plain Kotlin extension functions next to the type that owns the foreign shape, e.g. UserDto.toDomain() in the data module. They are static, trivially testable and need no DI. I would only use mapper classes if mapping needs injected dependencies like a clock or locale, and only use codegen (MapStruct is Java-centric) if hundreds of types repeat identical mappings. The real cost is not CPU, it is maintenance: every field added touches several mappers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Options:

Option Pro Con
Extension functions simple, discoverable, no DI cannot inject deps; scattered
Mapper class (@Inject) injectable (formatter, clock) DI binding per mapper
Codegen (MapStruct/KSP libs) less typing build cost, magic, verify KSP support

Rules: map at the boundary where the type enters (data layer maps DTO to domain; the ViewModel maps domain to UiModel). Never let a DTO cross the repository. Mapping lists is O(n); allocating n small objects is cheap on ART until n is large and mapped repeatedly (see the mapper performance scenario). Add a test per mapper using fixtures, especially for null/default handling.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun OrderEntity.toDomain() = Order(OrderId(id), Money(cents, currency), status = OrderStatus.from(statusCode))
fun Order.toEntity() = OrderEntity(id.value, total.cents, total.currency, status.code)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mapping inside the composable on every recomposition.
  • Lossy mappers (dropped fields) with no test.
  • Bidirectional mapping when you only need one direction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does an unknown enum value from the server go? → Map to an explicit Unknown case, never crash.
  2. Should domain-to-DTO exist? → Only for write paths that need it.
  3. How do you cut mapper count? → Share the model across layers when shapes truly match.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks one style. Senior ties the choice to injection needs, test strategy and field-add cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A new backend enum value crashed a mapper when with no else branch and hit 4% of sessions until an Unknown case was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A :domain module (Kotlin JVM, "pure") was reviewed after build times rose and a CI test began failing on JVM-only runs. Code:

// :domain/GetProfileUseCase.kt
import android.content.Context
import retrofit2.Response
import com.app.data.api.ProfileDto

class GetProfileUseCase(
    private val context: Context,
    private val api: ProfileApi,
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(): Profile {
        val res: Response<ProfileDto> = api.profile()
        val name = res.body()?.name ?: context.getString(R.string.unknown)
        return Profile(name)
    }
}

Crash seen in unit test: java.lang.RuntimeException: Method getString in android.content.Context not mocked. Also :domain now depends on :data and :app's R class.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Mock Context in the test." That hides a layering violation and keeps the module dependency inverted.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which module owns ProfileApi? Is the fallback string a business rule or a display choice? Who else calls this? Is :domain meant to be JVM-only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage; stop adding more imports. Add a CI check that fails if :domain has android.*/retrofit2.* imports.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Use case doing data work (calling API directly). (b) Presentation concern (localized string) in domain. (c) Convenience dependency from domain to data.
  4. How I'd verify: ./gradlew :domain:dependencies --configuration compileClasspath to see data/android on the classpath; grep imports; a Konsist rule.
  5. Root cause: Three boundary violations: domain depends on Android (Context), on a transport type (Response), and on data (ProfileDto). The arrow points outward.
  6. Fix: Short term: move retrofit call behind ProfileRepository (interface in domain, impl in data), return Profile? or a domain result. The "unknown" fallback becomes UI: ViewModel maps null name to stringResource. Long term: remove the dependency edge domain to data in Gradle so the compiler enforces it.
interface ProfileRepository { suspend fun profile(): Profile }
class GetProfileUseCase(private val repo: ProfileRepository) { suspend operator fun invoke() = repo.profile() }
  1. Prevention: Module deps that make illegal imports uncompilable; Konsist test; review checklist item "no android/retrofit/dto in domain".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep Context and mock it. I also would not keep this use case at all if it ends as pure delegation; a repository call from the ViewModel is enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Domain needs a localized message? → Return a typed reason (ProfileError.NotFound); UI maps to text.
  • Can domain use Dispatchers? → Yes, inject the dispatcher; it is a Kotlin library type.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found R imports in domain, which silently forced domain to be an Android library and slowed every unit test by a Robolectric start. Making it a kotlin("jvm") module broke the build in 6 places, which were exactly the leaks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Mocks Context, ignores layering.
  • Hire: Identifies the three leaks, moves API behind an interface.
  • Strong hire: Adds compile-time and test enforcement and questions whether the use case should exist.

questions.promptHtml: Where should the repository interface live and when are interfaces at layer boundaries worth it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates dependency inversion understanding from "interface for everything".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If I follow strict Clean Architecture, the interface lives in domain and the implementation in data, so data depends on domain. Interfaces at boundaries are worth it when there are real alternatives (fake in tests, multiple impls, KMP platform impls) or when I want the compiler to forbid dependencies. A single-implementation interface with no consumer needing isolation is ceremony.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reasons an interface earns its keep:

  1. Testing: a fake OrderRepository is simpler than mocking a concrete class; also, final classes in Kotlin need open/mockito-inline.
  2. Dependency direction: consumer owns the abstraction ("ports"); impl in another module can hide behind internal.
  3. Build: with an api/impl module split, consumers compile against a small API module, so impl changes do not recompile them.
  4. Multiplatform: common interface, platform impls.

Where it is waste: data sources used by exactly one repository and tested via that repository; mappers; ViewModel-owned helpers. Rule I use: introduce an interface at the boundary across a module or layer, not between collaborators inside one module.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :domain
interface SettingsRepository { val darkMode: Flow<Boolean> }
// :data (internal impl, bound in a Hilt module in :data)
internal class DataStoreSettingsRepository @Inject constructor(...) : SettingsRepository
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
internal interface SettingsBindings { @Binds fun bind(i: DataStoreSettingsRepository): SettingsRepository }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• IFooImpl-style one-to-one interfaces for every class.
  • Interface method signatures mirroring Retrofit/Room types.
  • Using @Binds module in the wrong Hilt component, so scoped instances duplicate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fake or mock? → Fake for repositories; mocks for verifying interactions only.
  2. How does internal help? → Hides impl classes so only the binding module sees them.
  3. Does an interface guarantee a good boundary? → No, leaky method signatures still couple you.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE interfaces everything. Senior places interfaces at module boundaries where they buy test, build, or direction benefits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An internal impl plus public interface let one team replace a SharedPreferences store with DataStore in a day without touching 30 callers.

questions.promptHtml: Package-by-layer or package-by-feature? What would you choose and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cheap signal of whether you think in features and ownership or in technical categories.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I package by feature, with layers inside the feature when needed. By-layer (ui/, data/, domain/ at the top) scatters one feature across the tree, so every change touches several packages and ownership is unclear. By-feature keeps related code together, makes deleting or extracting a feature easy, and maps naturally onto modules later.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
by-layer                      by-feature (layered inside)
ui/CartScreen.kt              cart/ui/CartScreen.kt
ui/CheckoutScreen.kt          cart/domain/AddToCart.kt
data/CartRepository.kt        cart/data/CartRepository.kt
data/OrderRepository.kt       checkout/ui/CheckoutScreen.kt
domain/AddToCart.kt           checkout/data/OrderRepository.kt

Benefits of by-feature: high cohesion, low coupling between features, internal visibility actually keeps things private, easy to turn a package into a Gradle module, fewer merge conflicts per team. The hybrid that scales: feature modules on top, shared core (design system, network, database) modules, and layering inside features if they are large. Now in Android follows a feature/core module split (verify the current layout in the repo).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Cross-feature imports of internals, defeating the structure.
  • One giant common/ or utils/ package that every feature depends on.
  • Splitting into layers inside a tiny feature with one class per layer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is by-layer fine? → Tiny apps, one team, few screens.
  2. How do shared things (user, session) fit? → In core/data modules owned by one team.
  3. How do you enforce feature isolation? → Modules, internal, Konsist/ArchUnit-style tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "cleaner". Senior ties it to ownership, deletability and module extraction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams moving from by-layer to modules found the migration costly because each feature's code was spread across five packages with cross-references.

questions.promptHtml: What are entities and value objects in the domain layer, and how do you model them in Kotlin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that "domain" means more than renamed DTOs and that you use the type system to make bugs impossible.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An entity has identity: two Users with the same id are the same user even if the name changed. A value object has no identity and is defined by its values: Money(100, "INR"). In Kotlin I model value objects as immutable data classes or @JvmInline value class, with validation in init or a factory, so invalid states cannot exist and primitives like raw String ids cannot be mixed up.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Entity equality: by id. Value object equality: structural.
  • Value classes (@JvmInline value class UserId(val value: String)) give type safety with no allocation in most usages; they box when used as nullable generics, in collections or interfaces, so they are not free everywhere. Value classes are stable since Kotlin 1.5.
  • Put business invariants where the data lives: Money refuses negative cents; Email validates format; OrderStatus as a sealed type with allowed transitions.
  • Do not confuse "Entity" in Clean Architecture with Room @Entity. Room entities are data-layer persistence models.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmInline value class UserId(val value: String)
data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) {
    init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative money" } }
    operator fun plus(o: Money): Money { require(currency == o.currency); return Money(minor + o.minor, currency) }
}
sealed interface OrderStatus { data object Placed : OrderStatus; data object Shipped : OrderStatus }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Anemic domain: data classes with no behavior and all rules in ViewModels.
  • Using Double for money.
  • Treating Room @Entity as the domain entity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Are data classes good entities? → Careful: equals compares all fields; override or compare by id where identity matters.
  2. Cost of value classes? → Boxing in generics/nullable; also mangled JVM names, awkward for Java interop.
  3. Where does validation of server data go? → At the mapper boundary; reject or default invalid data explicitly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines the terms. Senior shows invariants enforced in types and mentions boxing and equality pitfalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mix-up of two String ids (order vs user) passed compile for months until a value-class OrderId made it a compile error.

questions.contextHtml: A founder asks you to build the Android app for a 3-month MVP: 6 screens (login, list, detail, create, profile, settings), a REST API, 2 Android engineers, expected 5k users in the first quarter, schema likely to change weekly. A previous contractor's repo has domain, data, presentation modules, 74 files, 11 use cases that each call one repo method, and 4 model classes per entity. Time to add a field: about 2 hours. The founder says "make it clean and scalable". Release is in 10 weeks.
questions.promptHtml: What architecture do you pick and how do you justify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either "I'll use full Clean Architecture with multi-module, it's best practice", or "just put everything in the ViewModel". Both ignore cost and context.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Offline requirements? (decides SSOT and Room). Team growth in 12 months? iOS/KMP plans? Which business rules exist beyond CRUD? Is the API stable? What does "scalable" mean: users, features or people?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I would first cut the existing template down rather than adopt it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Mostly CRUD with little business logic: UI + data layers suffice. (b) A few rules (pricing, validation) could justify 1-3 use cases later. (c) Schema churn favors fewer mapped model types.
  4. How I'd verify: Count real logic: list rules per screen. Measure time to add a field. Review after 4 weeks for duplicated ViewModel logic.
  5. Root cause: The template optimizes for a team of 30 and low change rate, mismatching 2 engineers and weekly schema change.
  6. Fix: Single :app module (or :app + :core:designsystem if cheap), package-by-feature, Compose + ViewModel + Hilt, repositories with a DTO-to-domain mapper only where shapes differ, UiState per screen. Add use cases only when logic repeats. Keep repository interfaces to allow fakes.
  7. Prevention: Written triggers for evolving: split modules when build time passes ~1.5 min incremental or a second team starts; add a domain layer when two ViewModels share logic; enable an architecture test early.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not multi-module now (config overhead, slower iteration). Not skip layers entirely: keep data access out of composables so the later refactor is mechanical.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Founder: "We might raise and hire 15 engineers." → Layers by package and repository interfaces make module extraction a move operation later.
  • Investor wants iOS in 6 months? → Revisit KMP for data/domain; do not decide it blind now.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite startup took the contractor template; adding a "nickname" field took 8 files. They cut to 2 layers, shipped 3 weeks earlier, and extracted a domain module a year later only when a second client app appeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks full template or zero structure.
  • Hire: Picks UI + data, packages by feature, justifies.
  • Strong hire: Gives explicit upgrade triggers and tests assumptions with questions.

questions.promptHtml: Compare Clean, Hexagonal (ports and adapters) and Onion architectures. Are they different on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests breadth and whether you see the shared principle underneath the labels.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: All three invert dependencies so the business core depends on nothing and details depend on it. Hexagonal (Cockburn) frames it as ports (interfaces owned by the core) and adapters (UI, DB, network implementations). Onion (Palermo) arranges concentric layers with domain model at the centre. Clean (Martin) adds the explicit dependency rule and makes use cases first-class between entities and adapters. On Android they reduce to the same code shape: domain interfaces implemented by data and UI adapters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Hexagonal : [driving adapters: UI, tests] -> inbound ports -> CORE -> outbound ports <- [driven adapters: Room, Retrofit]
Onion     : Domain model -> domain services -> application services -> infra/UI (outermost)
Clean     : Entities -> Use cases -> Interface adapters (presenters, repos) -> Frameworks

Mapping to Android: ViewModel + Compose are driving adapters; Repository interface in domain is an outbound port; RepositoryImpl with Room/Retrofit is a driven adapter; use cases are the inbound port. Emphases differ: Hexagonal stresses symmetry (anything outside is an adapter), Onion stresses ranked layers, Clean stresses use cases and the rule. Critics note the sources largely agree and the debate is about labels; pick the vocabulary your team understands. Google's guide is a pragmatic variant with optional domain and directional layering.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debating names instead of explaining dependency direction.
  • Copying package names (usecases, ports) without inversion.
  • Believing one is "Android official".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a driving vs driven adapter? → Driving calls into the core (UI); driven is called by it (DB).
  2. Where do presenters sit in Clean? → Interface adapters; ViewModel acts as presenter/state holder.
  3. Is Android framework the outer ring? → Yes: Activity, Room and Retrofit are details.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists differences from memory. Senior states the invariant and maps all three onto the same Android shape.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team renamed packages to "ports/adapters" without any module boundary; Room annotations still leaked into ports, so nothing was actually hexagonal.

questions.contextHtml: CheckoutViewModel is 2,400 lines with 31 StateFlows, calls Retrofit services directly, computes discounts, tax and shipping, and formats strings. 3 teams edit it; merge conflicts weekly. Checkout is 100% of revenue (about 180k orders/day). Crash rate 0.9% on this screen, and CheckoutViewModelTest has 12 tests, 6 flaky. Two attempts at a full rewrite were abandoned. You may not freeze feature work, and any regression in totals is a sev-1.
questions.promptHtml: How do you decompose it safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite it in a new branch with Clean Architecture and swap." Big-bang, no verification, ignores the abandoned rewrites.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a flag system? Which logic is most volatile (discounts)? Do we have golden test data for totals? Are server-side totals authoritative?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze nothing, but add characterization tests for pricing on current behavior and CODEOWNERS split plans to cut conflicts; gate risky changes by flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pricing rules are the riskiest, extractable pure logic. (b) Direct API calls hide data-layer boundaries. (c) UI formatting inside VM bloats it. (d) 31 flows hint at 4-5 independent sub-states.
  4. How I'd verify: Group methods and flows by cohesion (call graph, IDE "extract" suggestions); coverage on pricing; track crash and totals-mismatch metrics per release; shadow compare old vs new outputs in production logs.
  5. Root cause: Absence of boundaries lets every change append to the nearest class; the VM is the only place that touches both UI events and APIs.
  6. Fix: Strangler steps, each shippable alone: (1) characterization tests; (2) extract pure CalculateTotalUseCase and call it from the VM; run old and new in parallel and log diffs; flip to new when diffs are zero; (3) extract CheckoutRepository behind an interface and move Retrofit; (4) split state holders per concern (address, payment, summary) as plain state holders owned by the VM; (5) move formatting into a UI mapper.
val legacy = legacyTotal(cart); val fresh = calculateTotal(cart)
if (legacy != fresh) analytics.logMismatch(cart.id, legacy, fresh) // old result still served
  1. Prevention: Size/complexity lint thresholds; CODEOWNERS per concern; architecture test that VMs do not import Retrofit.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang rewrite. Not new modules first: logic extraction first, modules after. Cost: 4-6 weeks of parallel run code.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Parallel run doubles compute? → Totals are cheap; sample 10% if needed.
  • Teams keep adding to the VM during migration? → Rule: new logic goes in the extracted classes only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's shadow compare caught a rounding difference (banker's vs half-up) on 0.04% of carts before any customer saw a wrong total.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang rewrite.
  • Hire: Incremental extraction with tests.
  • Strong hire: Shadow-compare pricing, flagged flips, ownership and lint to prevent regrowth.

questions.promptHtml: What rules should a use case follow about threads, state and lifecycle?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many use cases silently hold mutable caches or block the main thread.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A use case should be main-safe: callable from the main thread, moving CPU or blocking work to an injected dispatcher itself. It should be stateless: no mutable fields, no caching; state belongs in repositories or the UI layer. It has no lifecycle of its own and is scoped to the caller, so a new instance per consumer is fine and unscoped DI is the default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Google's guidance matches this: main-safe, single responsibility, no mutable data, instance per use. Concurrency policy belongs to the type doing the work, so inject dispatchers rather than hardcoding Dispatchers.Default, which makes tests deterministic with a TestDispatcher. Before adding withContext in a use case, ask whether the heavy work belongs in the data layer, especially if results should be cached and reused. Do not launch coroutines in the use case with a private scope; expose suspend or Flow and let the caller own cancellation. Use case holding a MutableStateFlow effectively becomes a hidden singleton once scoped wrongly.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SortPostsUseCase @Inject constructor(@DefaultDispatcher private val d: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(posts: List<Post>): List<Post> =
        withContext(d) { posts.sortedByDescending { it.score } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch inside the use case (leaked work, untestable).
  • @Singleton use case caching data.
  • Calling withContext(IO) around already main-safe suspend calls.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why inject dispatchers? → Tests, and swap policy centrally.
  2. Flow-returning use case: where is flowOn? → Inside, so collectors need not care.
  3. Where does a cache go? → The repository (SSOT).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use Dispatchers.IO". Senior says main-safe contract, injected dispatchers, statelessness and caller-owned scope.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cached @Singleton use case kept the previous user's data after logout, a privacy bug caught in QA.

questions.contextHtml: A trading-style list screen shows 5,000 Instrument rows from Room. The UI observes dao.observeAll(): Flow<List<InstrumentEntity>>; a repository maps to domain, a use case maps to InstrumentUiModel (formatting prices with NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance() per item), and the VM maps again. The table updates 4 times/second from a socket via DB writes. Symptoms on a mid-range device (4 GB RAM): scroll jank, 1,200 ms frame spikes on updates, heap growth with GC pauses (about 30 per minute in Profiler). Red herring: someone blames Compose recomposition.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without abandoning the layered models.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the layers and use the entity directly in the UI." Throws away structure instead of fixing hot-path allocations.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the whole list re-emitted on any row change? Which thread does mapping run on? Is the format object created per row?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle the DB-driven stream (sample(250)/conflate) and move mapping off main.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 3 full-list mappings x 4 Hz = 60,000 object creations per second plus formatter creation. (b) Mapping on main thread. (c) Whole-list emissions invalidate every row. (d) Recomposition (verify, not assume).
  4. How I'd verify: Android Studio CPU profiler/system trace for map frames and NumberFormat init; Allocation tracker; Compose layout inspector recomposition counts; Macrobenchmark frame timing.
  5. Root cause: NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance() is costly and was created 5,000 times per emission; each layer remapped the full list though only a few rows changed.
  6. Fix: Reuse one formatter; collapse the redundant domain-to-ui hop; map once on Dispatchers.Default via flowOn; provide stable keys and diff only changed rows; for tickers, query only visible ranges (paging) or hold per-row flows.
val ui: Flow<List<InstrumentUi>> = repo.observeAll()
    .sample(250)
    .map { list -> list.map { it.toUi(formatter) } }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
  1. Prevention: Benchmarks in CI on the list screen; a lint/review note on allocations in mappers; test with 10x list size.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sampling delays visible updates by up to 250 ms (acceptable for a ticker). I would not delete the domain model; I would drop a redundant mapping hop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users need real-time exactness for one row? → Per-row subscription for focused item.
  • Is 5,000 rows realistic on screen? → Paginate or virtualize; do not map all.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team cut p95 frame time from about 120 ms to 16 ms mostly by hoisting one formatter and sampling; the "layer overhead" suspicion was wrong.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames layers, removes them.
  • Hire: Profiles, finds allocation hot spot, offloads thread.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies, fixes emission rate and structure, adds benchmarks.

questions.promptHtml: Should the domain layer be a pure Kotlin/JVM module? What breaks when you try?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks practical module design, not just diagrams.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Ideally yes: a kotlin("jvm") module guarantees nothing Android can leak in and gives fast JVM tests. In practice friction appears: no @Parcelize, no Context, no R strings, no Paging 3 types (PagingData is from androidx.paging, which has a common/JVM artifact but verify), and Hilt injection annotations (javax.inject is pure JVM, so it works). I keep domain JVM-pure and accept small duplication; if too painful I use an Android library module but still ban android.* by rule.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• javax.inject.Inject is a plain JVM annotation, so @Inject constructor works in JVM modules; Hilt/Dagger codegen runs through kapt/KSP in the consuming Android module for @HiltViewModel, @InstallIn.
  • Kotlin coroutines and Flow are JVM/KMP libs: fine.
  • Pagination: a pure domain often exposes Flow<List<T>> or its own page abstraction; if you return PagingData you tie to AndroidX Paging (acceptable trade-off, but verify it compiles in your JVM module).
  • Strings: return typed results, not text.
  • Bonus: a JVM module is a step toward KMP commonMain.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// domain/build.gradle.kts
plugins { kotlin("jvm"); }
dependencies {
    implementation(libs.kotlinx.coroutines.core)
    implementation(libs.javax.inject)
    testImplementation(libs.kotlin.test)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Domain as com.android.library just for @Parcelize.
  • Pulling androidx.annotation casually (it is OK, but a slippery slope).
  • Using java.time below API 26 without desugaring (domain being JVM may hide this; verify desugaring in the app).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you pass domain models between screens? → Ids over navigation; load by id.
  2. Parcelable needed? → Map to a UI model with @Parcelize in the UI layer.
  3. Does a pure module slow builds? → It typically speeds tests and compile; fewer Android deps.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "pure Kotlin". Senior names the specific pain points and the workaround for each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A domain module on com.android.library accumulated Context usage within a year; converting it to JVM exposed 40 offenders.

questions.promptHtml: Should the UI layer be forbidden from talking to repositories directly, forcing everything through use cases?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Strict-rule vs flexible-rule judgment, which the Google guide explicitly leaves open.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I prefer the flexible rule: ViewModels may call repositories directly, and I add a use case only when there is logic to share or combine. Forcing everything through use cases guarantees domain logic cannot be bypassed (for example analytics on each access) but creates pass-through classes. If I notice the UI already reaches data almost exclusively through use cases, I then make it the rule.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Google's domain-layer page presents exactly this trade-off. Strict mode benefits: single enforcement point for cross-cutting policy (auditing, permission checks, logging), uniform code shape that new joiners learn once, and an architecture test can enforce it simply (ViewModels must not import repositories). Costs: trivial use cases, more files and DI bindings, indirection in navigation, and wrapper tests that verify delegation.

Decision factors: regulated domains (fintech, health) with audit requirements favor strict; small CRUD apps favor flexible. A middle path: strict only inside features with real logic. Whatever you choose, write it down and enforce it, because mixed styles inside one feature confuse.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixed styles within one screen: some calls via use case, others direct.
  • Strict rule without tooling, so reviewers argue per PR.
  • Using use cases to hide missing repository design.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you enforce strict mode? → Konsist/ArchUnit-style test on VM constructor parameter types, or module deps (UI module does not depend on data).
  2. How do you enforce flexible? → Review checklist and a lint on duplicated logic.
  3. How does the module graph reflect it? → UI module depending only on domain module makes strict compile-time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks a side. Senior chooses by risk profile and encodes it in module deps or tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A health app added an access-audit requirement and discovered 23 ViewModels hit repositories directly; with a strict rule it would have been one place.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace shows a discounted price on the product list, detail and cart. After a promo launch, support receives 1,900 tickets in 48 hours: "price changed at checkout". Cart total differs from the list price in 3.1% of sessions. Postmortem finds: ListViewModel applies price * (1 - promo) rounded with roundToInt(); DetailViewModel uses BigDecimal with HALF_UP; CartRepository applies the promo only for items added after the promo flag loaded. Unit tests exist for each class but none compare outputs. Red herring: the backend returned correct data.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review. What architectural cause and what changes do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fix the rounding in ListViewModel." Treats the symptom; the duplicated rule will drift again.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which component should be authoritative: client or server? Which promo rules exist? Which items/timing are affected? Is price display legally binding?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature flag to show server-computed prices (if provided) or hide client discount; hotfix to a single calculation function; communicate to support.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Same rule implemented in three places with different rounding. (b) Ordering bug: promo state loaded after cart items added. (c) Stale promo cache. (d) Backend (ruled out by payload diff).
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with fixture carts; log (itemId, promoVersion, computedPrice, source); compare across screens; check ordering with a test that loads the promo late.
  5. Root cause: Business logic lived in presentation/data classes, duplicated, with no single owner. Architecturally: a domain rule without a domain home.
  6. Fix: One Money value type with defined rounding and one ApplyPromotionUseCase (or domain Pricing function), used by all consumers; cart recomputes when promo state changes (derived from a promo flow, not a one-time snapshot). Prefer server-priced totals for checkout and show client price as an estimate.
class ApplyPromotion {
    operator fun invoke(price: Money, promo: Promo?): Money =
        promo?.let { price.times(BigDecimal.ONE - it.rate, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) } ?: price
}
  1. Prevention: Property/consistency tests across screens; an ADR assigning pricing ownership; metrics on client-vs-server total mismatch; flag the rollout.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just patch rounding in one VM. I would not compute authoritative money only on the client; the server must be the source of truth for payment.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not a shared util? → It lacks ownership and tests; a named domain object is discoverable and owned.
  • Rounding mode choice? → Match the backend/finance rule; verify, do not guess.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team added a "pricing contract" test fixture used by all three consumers and the backend; mismatch tickets dropped to near zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Patches one rounding site.
  • Hire: Centralizes logic in a use case.
  • Strong hire: Identifies ownership, state ordering, server authority, and prevention measures.

questions.contextHtml: In an interview you are asked: "Design the architecture for a news reader: feed with pull-to-refresh, offline reading, bookmarks, article detail, search. 2 teams of 4, 300k DAU." The interviewer says "keep it clean" and listens for what you do not do.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through your layering and say where you would stop.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Lists every pattern (Clean, MVI, modules, use cases for each call) without tying them to the requirements.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How fresh must the feed be? Bookmark sync across devices? Search local or server? Tablets? Offline duration? Rollout of feature teams?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I start with the simplest thing that satisfies offline and testing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Offline-first means DB is the single source of truth. (b) Two teams suggest feature split (feed/search vs bookmarks/detail). (c) Little real business logic besides merging bookmarks with articles.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype the feed path; measure cold start and scroll; check where logic duplicates across screens.
  5. Root cause: N/A: trade-off. Key idea: put boundaries where change and teams are.
  6. Fix (my design): UI layer: Compose screens + ViewModel with one UiState each. Data layer: ArticleRepository, BookmarkRepository backed by Room as SSOT, Retrofit for refresh. One use case, GetFeedWithBookmarksUseCase, because it combines two repositories. Mappers DTO to entity to domain. Hilt for DI. Modules: :app, :feature:feed, :feature:bookmarks, :core:data, :core:ui, :core:network, grown from packages when build time or ownership demands.
  7. Prevention: Fake repositories for tests; architecture test for layering; modularize when a second team's PRs conflict.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No use cases for plain reads; no separate UI model unless formatting is real; no MVI framework until state complexity warrants it; no per-class interfaces.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Now 1M DAU and 6 teams? → More feature modules, api/impl splits for cross-feature deps, convention plugins.
  • Search needs ranking? → Domain logic or server-side; decide by who owns the algorithm.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite candidate won the loop by stating the upgrade triggers (second team, build over 3 min, logic repeated twice) rather than pre-building them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Buzzword stack without reasoning.
  • Hire: Sound layers, SSOT, one justified use case.
  • Strong hire: Explicit non-goals, upgrade triggers, and testing strategy.

questions.contextHtml: A 40-engineer app (1.2M DAU) has VMs calling repositories directly. An architect mandates "all VMs go through use cases, new :domain module" and generates 210 use cases in one PR. Results after two releases: build time +45 s for incremental changes touching :domain; 180 of 210 use cases are one-line delegates; reviewers complain; two teams ignore the rule; one real bug: a use case marked @Singleton cached the previous account's cart after switching accounts (about 0.3% of sessions saw it).
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Enforce the rule harder" or "revert everything." Neither addresses value or the leak.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which use cases hold real logic? What drove the mandate (audit, duplication)? Who owns :domain? How is the build slowed (module placement or ABI changes)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the cart leak: remove @Singleton and clear on account switch; ship via staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Blanket mandate created low-value classes. (b) Statefulness in a use case violates the stateless rule. (c) :domain as one big module causes recompiles of all dependents on any change. (d) Teams ignoring the rule signals no perceived benefit.
  4. How I'd verify: Classify the 210 by logic (cyclomatic complexity, number of repos used); Gradle build scan to see recompilation causes; grep for mutable fields in use cases.
  5. Root cause: Process (bulk generation) over need; plus a stateful use case violating the contract.
  6. Fix: Keep the ~30 with logic or multi-repo combination; delete delegating ones, calling repositories directly; make stateful caching live in the repository keyed by account; split :domain by feature so changes recompile less; adopt "use case only when needed" rule with a lint for single-line delegates.
  7. Prevention: Konsist rule: use cases have no mutable properties; scope policy (no @Singleton on use cases); ADR describing when to add one.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not another mass PR. Remove gradually by feature, since mass deletions create merge risk. Accept lost uniformity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Auditors require all access through domain? → Then keep strict for those features, with justification.
  • Teams resist the reversal? → Present build-scan and bug data, not opinions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team measured: 14% of use-case files ever changed in a year; those were exactly the ones with logic. Deleting the rest removed 3,000 lines with no regression.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doubles down or panics.
  • Hire: Fixes leak, prunes delegates.
  • Strong hire: Data-driven triage, per-feature split, enforced stateless contract, ADR.

questions.subtopic: Limits of Clean Architecture on Android
questions.promptHtml: Where does textbook Clean Architecture fit Android poorly, and how do you adapt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors should know the pattern's failure modes, not only its benefits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The framework is not just a detail on Android: lifecycle, process death, Compose state and Paging shape the design. Strict domain purity fights tools like Room relations, Paging 3, and Flow-based UIs. Layer-by-layer modules also encourage horizontal slicing, hurting feature ownership. I adapt: keep the dependency rule where it pays (business rules, boundaries), allow pragmatic leaks (Paging types, coroutines), and slice modules by feature.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Friction points:

  • Process death/UI state: Domain says nothing about SavedStateHandle; state restoration is a presentation concern that textbook diagrams ignore.
  • Reactive data: Clean's request/response use cases predate Flow; modern use cases return streams, so "execute once" thinking breaks.
  • Paging/Room: Efficient lists want PagingSource and relations in the DB; mapping to pure domain models per page costs copies, and domain-level queries may duplicate what SQL does better.
  • Mapper tax: Four model types per entity for CRUD apps.
  • Horizontal modules: :domain, :data, :presentation for the whole app means every feature change edits all three; feature modules scale ownership better.
  • Over-fitting: Google's guide deliberately made the domain optional.

Adaptations: feature-first slicing; domain only where logic exists; accept Flow and selectively Paging in domain; keep Android types out of business rules but not out of the UI layer.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating the textbook as law instead of a set of trade-offs.
  • Abstracting Room away so fully that you lose transactions/relations.
  • Ignoring state restoration in "clean" diagrams.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Would you expose PagingData from domain? → Often yes as a pragmatic leak; the alternative costs copies.
  2. How do you evaluate success? → Change locality: how many files per typical change.
  3. What do you keep for sure? → The dependency rule at boundaries and testable business logic.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defends the pattern. Senior names concrete friction and shows which parts are worth keeping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fully layered app took 14 files per new field; after moving to feature slices with a thin domain, the typical change touched 4.
